About Me:

Medical student & PhD researcher specializing in biomedical data analysis, and research design. Experienced in developing eye-tracking research software and working with complex datasets.

Looking For Teammates:

Seeking UI/UX Designers, Web/App Developers, and Pitch Presenters looking to build an innovative, high-impact open-source prototype together. Everyone with enthusiasm is welcome!
summary:
Long-duration space missions create health challenges that astronauts cannot always address immediately with help from Earth. Changes in sleep, vital signs, immune function, and overall well-being can be difficult to recognize, especially when astronauts are busy with their daily responsibilities.

We built Cosmo to make health monitoring more accessible through conversation.

Instead of asking astronauts to navigate complicated forms or interpret medical charts on their own, Cosmo allows them to simply talk about how they feel and ask questions about their health. The assistant supports both Mongolian and English, provides daily health check-ups.
details:
The Problem

Astronauts operate in an environment where microgravity, isolation, workload, and distance from Earth can make health monitoring and communication challenging. A useful system should make it straightforward for crew members to report symptoms and changes in their condition, while helping support teams review those reports.

COSMO focuses on the interaction layer: making routine health check-ins and symptom reporting easier through voice and a clear interface.

How COSMO Works

1. Voice interaction: Crew members can interact with COSMO using voice, making the experience more natural and potentially reducing the need for lengthy manual input.

2. Daily check-ins: The prototype supports routine check-ins so crew members can report how they are feeling.

3. Health-change reporting: Crew members can describe changes in their condition and record health concerns.

4. Interactive pain reporting: The interface supports reporting pain and describing where it is occurring.

5. SOS alerts: The prototype includes an SOS-style alert pathway for urgent concerns. Any operational use would require validated escalation rules and integration with mission procedures.

6. Mission Control dashboard: A dashboard presents submitted information so a support team can review astronaut-reported health updates.

7. Research context: The project references NASA research datasets as context for exploring spaceflight health monitoring. Dataset references do not mean the prototype has been clinically validated against those datasets.

Technology
The project draft identifies the following technologies and services:

-Front end: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Recharts, and Framer Motion.

- Data storage: PostgreSQL and SQLite.

- Voice: ElevenLabs Scribe for speech input and ElevenLabs text-to-speech for spoken responses.

- AI: Claude API.

- Testing: Vitest.

- Visual assets: Two visual assets created with Higgsfield; the COSMO mascot uses original renders.


Source Code:
https://github.com/batlvndenbayrbileg-sys/cosmo


Why It Matters

A voice-first interface may make it easier for astronauts to communicate health concerns during demanding mission conditions. By bringing check-ins, symptom descriptions, and review tools into one prototype, COSMO demonstrates one possible approach to more accessible health communication between crew members and mission support teams.

The long-term opportunity is to explore how such tools could complement—not replace—established medical protocols, trained personnel, and validated monitoring systems.
